The Golden Age of Spain. Or Siglo de Oro, the "century of gold," encompasses the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries when Spain achieved unprecedented power, wealth, and cultural brilliance.

Fueled by New World gold and imperial expansion, Spanish kingdoms produced a dazzling literary and artistic efflorescence. This was the era of Cervantes, Lope de Vega, and Velázquez.

Politically, Spain unified under Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella in the late fifteenth century. They conquered Granada, ending Al-Andalus, sponsored Columbus, and built a transatlantic empire spanning the Americas, Philippines, and Mediterranean.

Gold and silver from the New World, especially the Potosí mines, flooded Spanish treasuries. This funded armies, architecture, and the patronage of the arts on an unprecedented scale.

Literature flourished. Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote in 1605, often called the first modern novel. Lope de Vega composed over one thousand plays. Poets like Luis de Góngora and Francisco de Quevedo experimented with baroque complexity.

Spanish mysticism produced profound spiritual writers like Saint Teresa of Ávila and Saint John of the Cross. Their works remain touchstones of European spirituality and literature.

Visual arts reached sublime heights. El Greco, a Cretan painter working in Toledo, created visionary religious canvases. Diego Velázquez produced court paintings of unprecedented psychological depth.

The Counter-Reformation shaped Spanish culture profoundly. The Inquisition persecuted Muslims, Jews, and heterodox thinkers, driving intellectual conformity even as individual genius found expression in permitted forms.

By the seventeenth century's end, Spanish military power had waned through defeats in the Thirty Years' War and loss of naval supremacy. The economy declined, yet cultural production continued at high levels.

The Golden Age represented the convergence of imperial wealth, religious fervor, intellectual ambition, and artistic genius—a moment when Spain led European civilization before passing that role to France and eventually to Atlantic powers.
